data.title: Trump’s SEC nominee Johnson backs formal rulemaking for tokenized stock trading
data.description:
President Donald Trump’s nominees to fill two vacancies at the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) faced questions about investor protections, regulatory oversight and financial innovation during a Senate confirmation hearing Thursday, including scrutiny of the agency’s approach to tokenized securities.

Kristin Johnson, Trump’s Democratic nominee, backed formal rulemaking to address concerns about the agency’s exemption for tokenized stock trading.

“I feel strongly that regulation is made better through the notice and comment period,” Johnson told the Senate Banking Committee in response to Democratic Senator Angela Alsobrooks. She added that she would welcome the opportunity to address issues covered by the exemption through that process.

The SEC’s Sept. 17 exemption lets qualifying platforms trade blockchain-based versions of US-listed shares without registering as securities exchanges under certain conditions. The order took effect immediately and invites comments on possible changes.

Johnson, a former Commodity Futures Trading Commission commissioner, appeared alongside Republican Steven Levine, a former aide to SEC Commissioner Mark Uyeda. If confirmed, they would bring the five-member commission to four members, with three Republicans and one Democrat.

The hearing comes as the SEC has scaled back enforcement activity and pursued regulatory changes intended to accommodate digital assets, including efforts to facilitate tokenized securities that have drawn scrutiny from lawmakers and market participants.

Companies reject tokenized stock listings

The measure has drawn objections from publicly traded companies, with 67 opposing the tokenization of their shares on the OKXICE platform, according to a Nov. 5 public notice.

Johnson also cited concerns about Anti-Money Laundering and Know Your Customer compliance, noting that objections to the exemption extended beyond investor protection.

Levine, meanwhile, said he had not closely studied the innovation exemption but understood it to be time-limited and include investor protections. He emphasized that Congress had authorized the SEC to grant exemptions from federal securities laws when doing so serves the public interest and remains consistent with investor protection requirements.

He pointed to exchange-traded funds as an example of financial innovation that initially developed through regulatory exemptions before becoming subject to broader agency rules.

Senate weighs bipartisan SEC appointments

If confirmed, Johnson would become the SEC’s only Democratic commissioner, a development some in the crypto industry believe could strengthen the agency’s approach to regulation.

“Crypto isn’t a partisan issue, and the rules that come out of a bipartisan commission will stand on firmer footing,” Jessica Martinez, US policy director at digital asset infrastructure company Fireblocks, told Cointelegraph.

Martinez added that even minority commissioners can influence policy by challenging proposals and pushing for unresolved issues to be addressed before rules are finalized.

Senators have until noon Friday to submit additional written questions to the nominees, with responses due by 5:00 pm ET on Nov. 24, according to the committee’s closing remarks.

The nominations could then advance to a committee vote before being considered by the full Senate. Both nominees would require Senate confirmation before taking their seats at the SEC.

data.title: It’s a ‘dark period for tech’ as Anthropic debuts IPO – Dan Ives
data.description:
Anthropic's public debut marks a watershed moment for the technology sector even as broader markets endure what Dan Ives, co-partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co., called "a dark period for tech" in an interview with CNBC.

While the AI company's IPO demonstrated strong institutional appetite during its roadshow, the S&P 500 (SP500) has fallen for six consecutive days, and the entire AI stock stack has pulled back sharply.

Ives described the current market environment as "a tale of two cities," with Anthropic's successful offering standing in stark contrast to widespread investor anxiety.

He attributed the tech sector's struggles to concerns surrounding Nvidia and China, as well as broader uncertainty that has sent the VIX Volatility Index to 28—its highest level since March.

Despite the turbulence, Ives characterized the downturn as "a panic moment" rather than a fundamental shift in the technology landscape.

"We're less than 15% through the build out of the AI revolution," he said, adding that the foundational bull thesis for tech remains intact.

The analyst emphasized that Anthropic's IPO could pave the way for OpenAI's expected public offering in early 2027, underscoring the continued momentum in artificial intelligence development.

He noted that if Anthropic succeeds in generating substantial annual revenue over the next five to seven years, the company could see its valuation grow significantly.

Ives pointed to expected capital expenditure growth as a key driver for the sector, projecting $1.3T to $1.5T in AI infrastructure spending next year. Anthropic , he said, will be "a huge piece of that" alongside other frontier AI models and companies in cybersecurity and software.

Looking ahead, Ives suggested that the current market anxiety will eventually be viewed as a buying opportunity.

"I think we're going to look back in this period, just like April 2025 Liberation Day, and March 2020 during COVID as the opportunity," he said, dismissing comparisons to the 2007 bubble given current valuations and growth fundamentals.

data.title: Meta to price Muse Charm gadget at $300, The Information reports
data.description:
Meta Platforms plans to price its pocket-sized AI device, Muse Charm, at $300 and offer buyers up to 12 months of free 5G data from Verizon , the Information reported on Thursday, citing a person familiar with the matter.

  • Meta and Verizon did not immediately respond to Reuters' requests for comment

  • The device that carries the viral Muse AI agent into the real world was unveiled in September by chief executive Mark Zuckerberg during the company's annual conference

  • Muse Charm underscores Meta's broader push to reduce its reliance on Apple and Google's operating systems by building its own AI platform

  • Users can tap the gadget to access Muse directly, bypassing AI apps on their smartphones

  • The device features a roughly 2-inch (5-cm) screen that can be navigated with a thumb, with a customizable Muse character at its center

  • A built-in 5G modem allows access to Muse even without Wi-Fi, though it cannot make call

  • Muse has gained traction among users as Meta expands its push to make its AI assistant a more widely used consumer service

  • The AI agent allows users to delegate tasks such as shopping, travel booking and form-filling to an AI agent

  • Meta is expected to launch Charm in time for the holiday shopping season in December, according to Zuckerberg's comments at the company's Connect event.

data.title: Visa, Mastercard and JPMorgan Customer Data Leaked by Hackers — WSJ
data.description:
By Ben Glickman and Alexander Saeedy

Data from thousands of customers of Visa, Mastercard and JPMorgan Chase was leaked Thursday by a ransomware group, the latest in a string of tech incidents that have unnerved consumers in the last week.

A Visa spokesman said no payments data, such as card numbers, were affected and Visa's own systems weren't involved or affected. It added that the incident involved a third-party service provider in the Asia-Pacific region.

A Mastercard spokesman said the incident exposed a "limited amount of information from a subset of cardholders enrolled in a specific benefit program" He added that the exposure has been contained and that there is no impact on Mastercard's payment network or the ability of people to use their cards.

A JPMorgan spokeswoman said that third parties who provide services to the firm were targeted, and the company believes attackers accessed marketing data, potentially including customer names and email addresses. The bank said there was no disruption to its customer services.

A ransomware hacking group called n0n has claimed responsibility for the attack, according to cybersecurity firm SOCRadar.

None of the firms named the third-party company that was hacked.

The companies have millions of customers, but the hack comes as anxiety has run high about the ability of artificial-intelligence to supercharge cyberattacks and a series of tech failures spooked Americans.

Earlier this week, customers for JPMorgan Chase experienced issues accessing their accounts and sending payments, which the bank said was the result of a software update. The issue rippled across into complaints about other banks, raising fears among consumers and across the internet of widespread banking turbulence. Coupled with the Federal Aviation Administration's decision to temporarily ground all flights on Friday and an earlier disruption at Microsoft that kept people out of their emails, the country was on edge about the safety of technology critical to daily life.

"There is no connection to service disruption of some customers experienced earlier this week," JPMorgan Chase's statement said Thursday.

Write to Ben Glickman at ben.glickman@wsj.com and Alexander Saeedy at alexander.saeedy@wsj.com

data.title: Amodeis Sidestep Question on Jensen Huang — WSJ
data.description:
By Maxwell Zeff

Anthropic cofounders Dario and Daniela Amodei declined to say whether they thought former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang should be reinstated during an interview with CNBC. "That's up to Nvidia," said Dario. When asked what they made of the ouster, the Amodeis cited their policy difference with Huang and work with other chip partners.

"We've been a partner to Nvidia for a long time. We work with them on data centers. We've had a long and productive partnership with them. Of course, we're not always going to agree on policy issues with our partners," Dario said.

Daniela added that Anthropic is unique in the quantity of partners it works with for compute, including Google, Broadcom and Amazon. "I do think this has been a helpful strategic advantage for us," she said of the diversity.

Anthropic has occasionally found itself at odds with Huang. Earlier this year, Dario wrote in an essay that it would be helpful for the U.S. government to help the tech industry collectively slow the development of AI models, in order to avoid antitrust concerns. Huang responded at the time by saying new laws or regulations for AI companies to properly release their products was "completely unnecessary".

This item is part of a Wall Street Journal live coverage event. The full stream can be found by searching P/WSJL (WSJ Live Coverage).

data.title: NASA probe achieves light-day milestone and is 'not done yet'
data.description:
Key points:
  • US space agency marks Voyager 1's historic achievement
  • NASA says radio signal from probe confirmed its location
  • A light-day is about 16 billion miles (26 billion km)
  • Voyager 1 probe is the most distant human-made object

By Will Dunham

NASA confirmed on Thursday its Voyager 1 probe has achieved an unprecedented distinction — becoming the first spacecraft to travel beyond a light-day from Earth — even as the aging probe runs low on power and experiences technical anomalies in a mission one official promised is "never going to end."

A radio signal sent by the robotic explorer from interstellar space was received in Madrid through the Deep Space Network, NASA's international array of radio antennas, showing the probe had reached the milestone after 49 years, 2 months and 11 days of flight..

Voyager 1 passed the distance that light travels in a day — about 16 billion miles (26 billion km) — as expected on Wednesday at 5:16 a.m. EST (1016 GMT), NASA said, with the signal taking about a day to reach Earth. Voyager 1 is the most distant human-made object.

NASA engineer Nshan Kazaryan announced the confirmation, saying at a Jet Propulsion Laboratory facility in California, "After 16 billion miles of exploration, Voyager 1 continues its journey into the unknown."

NASA officials and mission leaders celebrated the achievement even as they acknowledged the spacecraft's frailty.

"This is such an amazing day," Nicola Fox, NASA's head of science, told a JPL event, lauding the team "that just continues to let Voyager keep on trekking out there."

A light-year may be a more familiar concept for many people, a metric used for enormous cosmic distances. It is the distance a particle of light, called a photon, travels in a year — about 5.9 trillion miles (9.5 trillion km).

"When's the mission going to end? It's never going to end, even when we can no longer talk to Voyager," Fox said, as the probe traverses the near-vacuum of interstellar space, the vast expanse between stars.

It is currently flying in the direction of the star Gliese 445, some 17 light-years from Earth, and would pass within about 1.7 light-years of it in about 40,000 years if the probe keeps its current pace.

Voyager 1 is flying at almost 38,000 miles per hour (61,000 kph). It crossed the outer edge of the heliosphere, a protective bubble of particles and magnetic fields produced by the sun, to enter ‌interstellar space ⁠in 2012. It journeyed past Jupiter and Saturn, the solar system's two largest planets, earlier in its mission.

Its twin, Voyager 2, was also launched in 1977 and entered interstellar space in 2018.

SIGNS OF AGE

As one might expect, Voyager 1 is showing signs of its age. It stopped transmitting science and engineering data last week, though it has remained in contact with Earth. Voyager project manager Suzanne Dodd expressed confidence that it would resume transmitting this data.

"And, meanwhile, we're running out of power," Voyager mission manager Kareem Badaruddin said.

A JPL representative said this week that recent power-saving measures could give the two Voyager spacecraft enough power to stay in communication with Earth for three to four more years.

"The anomalies have become normal for us," Badaruddin said.

"We're having to work with today's technology to interface with aging technology — aged technology — and just solving problems that way," Badaruddin said.

Voyager 1 is collecting data on, among other things, the effects from the sun such as solar storms that cause shocks and pressure fronts that extend as far away as the probe's current location, and fast-moving energetic particles called galactic cosmic rays in interstellar space.

"We're one light-day, but we are definitely not done yet," Dodd said.

Voyager 2, launched a few weeks before its twin, is "very healthy," Dodd said. It is expected to reach the light-day distance in November 2035.

NASA has turned off instruments on both Voyager probes to conserve diminishing electrical power from their decaying plutonium power sources and keep them operating. Voyager project scientist Linda Spilker said Voyager 1 is down to two instruments and Voyager 2 down to three.

"They're in an area of space that we've never been to, so every single bit of data that comes back is precious," Fox said.

Fox spoke of the possibility of sending nuclear-powered probes for further study of the conditions in interstellar space.

"What you want is a lot of power," Fox said.

Voyager deputy project scientist Jamie Rankin sees an optimistic message in Voyager 1's persistence.

"I think that this should be a reminder to all of us," Rankin said, "that no matter how long it takes or how dark things get, or what we think our limitations are, we should never stop shining and never stop reaching for the stars — for we never know how far we will go."

data.title: U.S. Diesel Prices to Continue to Fall in Relief for Consumers, U.S. Energy Secretary Says - Update
data.description:
By Adam Whittaker

WARSAW--U.S. diesel prices are likely to continue falling from record highs as refined products from the Persian Gulf return to the market and unsanctioned Russian diesel adds to the downward pressure on prices, according to U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright.

"The trajectory we're on right now is downward for the foreseeable future," Wright said in an interview on the sidelines of the Partnership for Transatlantic Energy Cooperation conference in Warsaw. This trajectory, however, depends on nothing "big or bad" happening, he cautioned.

The U.S. temporarily removed sanctions on Russian diesel earlier this year to add supply to an extraordinarily tight fuel market. To date, no Russian diesel has arrived in the U.S. and several fuel tankers bound for America have shifted course after struggling to find buyers willing to accept the cargoes.

Regardless of whether Russian diesel lands in the U.S., the return of the country's fuel to the global market puts downward pressure on the price U.S. consumers pay at the pump, Wright said.

In September, the national average price of diesel hit $6.53 a gallon, the highest on record, according to the American Automobile Association. Prices have since eased to $5.93 a gallon on Thursday, but remain above the average price of $3.78 a year ago.

Global conflicts this year have upended energy and fuel markets.

Attacks on energy infrastructure in the Persian Gulf and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz have crippled exports from the region. A series of workarounds and pipelines has seen crude oil exports roar back but refined products have been slower to return.

At the same time as conflict raged in the Gulf, Ukrainian missile and drone attacks on Russian refineries further crimped global diesel supply. The fuel, which is at the heart of the American economy, soared and put pressure on households and businesses just before the mid-term election, when Democrats stripped Republicans of congressional control.

If European allies had been much more proactive releasing fuel from strategic reserves to the market, U.S. diesel prices would never have risen into the $6.50's a gallon, Wright said.

The U.S. strategic reserves predominantly consist of crude oil whereas European countries hold significant amounts of diesel and refined products, Wright added.

"I wish we'd got better cooperation from our friends and allies in Europe," he said.

The continent was "remarkably reluctant to release their diesel stores despite their promises to do so," Wright said. "That led to prices going higher than they should have gone," he added.

The conflict in the Gulf has put energy security at the top of governments' agendas. Several countries are looking to put more oil and products into strategic reserves in different locations around the world.

The U.S. holds a tiny amount of diesel in reserves, and released a third of the roughly 1 million barrels held going into the conflict, Wright said.

As part of a review of its strategic reserves, the U.S is considering increasing how much diesel it holds for emergencies. Growing its diesel reserves is a very reasonable idea, and a very real possibility, Wright said.

"Can we count on [Europe] in the future, or do we need to build our own diesel reserve?" he asked.

Write to Adam Whittaker at adam.whittaker@wsj.com

data.title: Could Huang, Nvidia and company's board be held liable over affair scandal?
data.description:
By Tom Hals

Reports that Jensen Huang, the co-founder of AI chip powerhouse Nvidia, had an extramarital affair with a company executive and ties to a suspected Chinese spy have led to his resignation as CEO and sparked investigations by the US securities regulator and FBI, calls for congressional hearings, a review by the company's independent directors and a proposed investor class action lawsuit.

Below is a look at the potential legal exposure for Huang, Nvidia and the directors of the company, which dominates the global market for computer chips that power the AI economy.

WHAT ARE THE ALLEGATIONS?

Huang had a relationship with Alice Huang, an unrelated former executive of ​Singapore-based company Megaspeed, and US intelligence agencies are trying to determine her ties to China's Ministry of State Security, according to two people familiar with the matter. Megaspeed has faced US scrutiny over suspicions that it helped Beijing gain access to Nvidia's advanced AI chips that are subject to US export restrictions.

Huang admitted he was unfaithful to his wife without providing details about the relationship, which led to a drop in Nvidia's stock price. US President Donald Trump said Huang told him that he had no idea that the woman was a spy and Huang has not been accused of criminal wrongdoing.

Reuters could not independently verify the intelligence allegation, which China's foreign ministry has said was "groundless."

Nvidia formed an independent committee of directors that hired the Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to assist in an internal investigation.

Huang resigned on November 11 after reports that he had an extramarital affair with a company executive who reported to him.

Nvidia sits at the center of the ​technological rivalry between the United States and China. Washington has imposed restrictions on exports of advanced AI chips to China since ​2022. News of the affair has emerged as Democrats seized control of Congress in the November 3 midterm elections, propelled in part by anti-AI and anti-corruption sentiment.

WHAT ABOUT FEDERAL SECURITIES FRAUD?

A proposed class action was filed in San Jose, California, federal court on November 9 alleging the company and Huang defrauded shareholders by concealing Huang's alleged relationship with Alice Huang and Megaspeed, which Jensen Huang described in an October 30 Bloomberg interview as "normal and not unusual."

Securities fraud plaintiffs must show that Nvidia and Huang knowingly misled investors, that investors relied on those misleading statements and that those misleading statements artificially inflated the stock.

The lawsuit did not specify damages but the stock lost around 20% from its peak to the end of the class period, a decline of around $1 trillion in market value.

Such lawsuits are often filed in the wake of a company's stock suffering a large drop, and more are likely.

While the vast majority of US public companies have insurance against securities lawsuits, Nvidia does not given its huge financial resources.

WHAT ABOUT STATE LAW VIOLATIONS?

Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway, a Republican, is investigating whether Huang’s actions harmed state pension funds and her office said they were looking at it through a consumer protection lens focused on potential misrepresentations.

California Attorney General Rob Bonta told Bloomberg that the Nvidia crisis raised red flags and his office could investigate. Bonta's office did not respond to a request for further details.

State officials could use state securities laws to pursue investigations of alleged violations, according to legal experts. New York's Martin Act is considered the most powerful and the state's attorneys general have used it to police Wall Street, including an insider trading case brought this year. The Martin Act also allows the attorney general to pursue criminal claims.

No states have brought claims and the New York attorney general did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

COULD THE SEC STEP IN?

The US Securities and Exchange Commission launched a civil investigation that included whether Nvidia misled investors, the Wall Street Journal reported, citing people familiar with the situation. Reuters has not verified the report.

The regulator would have a lower burden of proof than a private investor class action and the SEC can obtain alternative remedies, such as barring individuals from serving as officers or directors of public companies.

In 2022, during the administration of Democratic President Joe Biden, Nvidia settled allegations by the SEC that in 2018 it had made inadequate disclosures regarding the growth of its processors for the gaming market. The company paid a $5.5 million fine but did not admit or deny the allegations. An investor class action lawsuit over the same allegations is ongoing.

The SEC declined to comment.

COULD THE BOARD BE HELD LIABLE?

An investor filed a so-called derivative lawsuit on November 11 seeking to hold the board liable for failing to make a good faith effort to oversee the business and Huang. The lawsuit said the board allowed Nvidia to make repeated assurances about the company's dealings with Megaspeed and the board did not act on warning signs about Huang's relationship with Alice Huang until it was public.

The lawsuit, filed in federal court in the Northern District of California, also said the board lacked independence to investigate Huang.

Huang's resignation could strengthen the board's defenses against derivative lawsuits by showing the directors were acting on signs of misconduct by forcing him out and refusing to consider his return.

Investors, including state pension funds, can also use their shareholder rights to seek internal records to investigate the board and look for potential conflicts.

The board could sue Huang for any fines or securities fraud settlements that result from the scandal. For example, electric truck maker Nikola took legal action and got a judgment of $168 million against its former CEO Trevor Milton.

CAN SECURITIES FRAUD CARRY CRIMINAL PENALTIES?

Only a small fraction of all securities fraud cases lead to criminal charges, as most violations are handled through civil or administrative enforcement.

But a federal statute, enacted as part of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002, criminalizes schemes that knowingly defraud investors through false pretenses. Prosecutors would need to show that Huang intentionally lied to the public about the affair in order to keep Nvidia's stock price from falling, rather than for personal reasons such as avoiding embarrassment.

US Attorney General Todd Blanche also said the FBI was investigating if Alice Huang was a spy.

If Huang knew about Alice Huang’s alleged intelligence connection, he could face criminal liability under the Economic Espionage Act, a 1996 law that punishes the misappropriation of trade secrets to benefit a foreign government.

data.title: Spire downgraded at Jefferies ahead of rate case outcomes
data.description:
Spire slipped 1.6% in Thursday's trading as Jefferies downgraded the natural gas utility to Hold from Buy with an unchanged $94 price target, saying recent wins leave a more balanced risk/reward while remaining constructive on the company's longer-term earnings profile.

Spire shares have moved from local distribution company laggard earlier this year to the sector's strongest performer over the past three months, leaving fewer near-term catalysts to drive the stock higher, Jefferies analyst Julien Dumoulin-Smith said.

The company's portfolio has transitioned toward a cleaner regulated gas utility mix, with Tennessee providing a constructive growth jurisdiction and Missouri Gas adding contracted pipeline earnings, Dumoulin-Smith said, forecasting a 7.3% FY 2028-31 earnings per share compound annual growth rate, modestly above the 7% guidance midpoint, with the Missouri recovery supporting the FY 2028 step-up.

The Missouri rate case remains the largest FY 2028 swing factor, according to the analyst, who modeled $111M, or ~65%, of the $171M of Spire's  net new request, supporting a 9.8% earned return on equity.

Following the stock's recent outperformance, the analyst said he awaits greater visibility on Missouri's execution and balance sheet improvement before turning more positive.

Other tech stocks aren't faring as well. Advanced Micro Devices is down 7.4% and SpaceX has declined 4%. The tech-heavy Nasdaq is down 1.5%, while the S&P 500 has declined 1.4% and the Dow Jones Industrial Average has is off 1.7%.

Gold slide to a new 52-week low, declining 1.46% to $3682.10 per troy ounce on Thursday, reaching lowest settle value since September 2025. The dollar strengthened against major peers.

Brent oil prices inched up 0.24% after falling in recent days. Concerns about the Middle East conflict are persisting, but improving global supply is helping limit oil price gains.

data.title: Crude Oil Inches Higher Amid Ongoing Hormuz Crisis, Concerns Over Possible U.S. Attacks On Iran
data.description:
WASHINGTON (dpa-AFX) - Giving up the gains made earlier in the session, crude oil prices have edged higher on Thursday as fears of supply disruptions increased after Iranian military continued to announce vessels hitting naval mines and catching fire while transiting the Strait of Hormuz. However, the upside movement was limited as investors assessed the surplus supply outlook projected by the International Energy Agency.

WTI Crude Oil for December delivery was last seen trading up by $0.17 (or 0.20%) at $83.43 per barrel.

The navy of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps announced that two supertankers, which were escorted by U.S. jets, hit naval mines while attempting to transit through the southern part of the Strait of Hormuz which Iran has designated as an 'unauthorized route'. Reportedly, the tankers caught fire.

The information was reported by Iran's state media Tasnim as well as the Associated Press.

Both the tankers were carrying a total of more than 4 million barrels of crude oil.

The claims by Iran about vessels hitting the naval sea-mines planted by Iran have not been completely corroborated. However, market participants are pricing in supply disruptions in the near-term.

After shutting the Strait of Hormuz immediately after the U.S.-Israel joint attacks began on Iran in late February, the control over the Strait of Hormuz remains uncertain with both the U.S. and Iran making claims and counter-claims over its management.

Iran already warned fleet owners to comply with Iranian military's guidelines and not to navigate through the seaway which could expose them to mine-threats.

Yesterday, in an interview with Fox News, U.S. President Donald Trump stated that there are indications that Iran may be working to develop biological or chemical weapons since the U.S. successfully shut down its nuclear programs.

Elsewhere in the Middle East, the Saudi-led coalition stated that it intercepted a Houthi cruise missile fired towards southern Saudi Arabia.

Yesterday, the New York Times reported that Trump is weighing another round of extensive military strikes against Iran.

The report added that Israel has provided the U.S. with its intelligence findings suggesting that Iran has remade its drone and missile arsenals, and advancing its chemical and biological weapons programs.

On the inventory front, last Friday, in one of its key findings, the Paris-based International Energy Agency reported that the global oil market will return to a surplus in the fourth quarter of 2026. It added that the supply will add around 105 million barrels per day, 1.70 million bpd higher than the earlier forecast for demand.

According to the report, despite the threat in shipping the output, oil-producing gulf nations have found alternative routes to export their products to their respective destinations.

Today, at a press conference, the IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol commented that the energy world will not go back to what it was before the war started.

The U.S. dollar index was last seen trading at 103.89, up by 0.03 (or 0.03%) today.

data.title: Law firm Kirkland performed $11.8 million in free legal work for Trump administration, Democrats say
data.description:
Key points:
  • House and Senate Democrats investigating law firms' pro bono work for administration
  • Kirkland disclosed free work for US Commerce and Defense Departments
  • Probe expected to intensify following Democrats' midterm victories

By Mike Scarcella and David Thomas

US congressional Democrats probing law firms that made deals with President Donald Trump's administration said on Thursday that Kirkland & Ellis has provided at least $11.8 million in free legal services to federal agencies, calling it evidence of a "corrupt bargain" with the White House.

Democrats in the House and Senate are ramping up scrutiny of nine major law firms' agreements with Trump last year to provide nearly $1 billion in free legal services in order to avoid executive orders targeting firms over their legal work, diversity policies and ​political affiliations.

Trump issued the executive orders early in his second term, part of a broader campaign of retribution against his perceived political enemies.

Kirkland performed about $4 million in pro bono work for the US Commerce Department and $2.2 million for the US Defense Department, US Representative Jamie Raskin and US senators Richard Blumenthal and Adam Schiff said in a statement.

The firm also provided free legal services to the US Postal Service and US International Development Finance Corporation, they said.

"The Trump Administration also unsuccessfully tried to involve Kirkland & Ellis in work supporting the President’s political vanity projects, such as the renaming of the Kennedy Center or supporting the illegal construction of his triumphal arch in Washington, D.C. — raising serious questions of whether other firms acceded to these demands,” the lawmakers said in a statement.

Kirkland did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Trump said in April 2025 that the firm had agreed to provide $125 million in pro bono work to causes he supported.

FIRM'S DISCLOSURE TO LAWMAKERS

The firm, in a November 5 letter to the lawmakers seen by Reuters, said it had billed a total of more than $18.7 million in pro bono work relating to its deal with Trump, amounting to more than 15,000 hours of attorney work for the federal government and other clients.

The firm disclosed the figures in response to requests from the Democratic lawmakers, who have vowed to continue their investigation in the next Congress. Democrats' sweeping victory in the November midterm elections will give them additional power to demand documents and testimony from the law firms about their deals and how the administration has sought to enforce them.

Raskin currently serves as the ranking member of the House Judiciary Committee. Blumenthal is ranking member of the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations.

NEGOTIATIONS WITH WHITE HOUSE

Kirkland said in its letter that it began negotiating with the Trump administration after rival firm Skadden reached its own deal in March 2025.

Kirkland said its White House agreement has had "little impact" on its pro bono work, telling lawmakers that the firm "still devotes substantial pro bono resources to interests that could be considered 'progressive.'"

The law firm is represented by prominent Washington litigator Beth Wilkinson of Wilkinson Stekloff. She did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The law firms' agreements came after Trump issued executive orders targeting four firms. The orders sought to revoke lawyers' security clearances, restrict their access to federal buildings and end US government contracts held by the firms' clients.

Four judges ⁠last year struck down the orders, finding they violated the firms' constitutional free-speech and due-process rights. The Trump administration is appealing those rulings.

data.title: Corn, wheat bounce from multi-month lows, soybeans slump
data.description:
By Karl Plume

US corn and wheat futures firmed on Thursday in a short-covering bounce from multi-month lows, while soybeans drifted lower for a fourth straight session on technical selling and as the Brazilian real weakened.

Wheat drew additional strength from worries about shipments from the Black Sea region amid an absence of diplomatic progress towards de-escalation in Russia's war in Ukraine during three-way talks between the United States, Russia and China.

Grain markets moderated after tumbling earlier this week on a strengthening US dollar, which triggered broad-based selling across commodity markets.

"Today it's just profit taking taking after corn pushed to new lows. I can argue that on the wheat side, there is a fundamental discussion because Putin basically closed the door completely on any Ukraine ceasefire," said Rich Nelson, chief strategist at Allendale Inc.

Chicago Board of Trade December corn rose 3-1/2 cents to $4.39 a bushel after earlier touching its lowest point since June 30. CBOT December wheat was up 8-1/4 cents at $5.78-1/4 a bushel after hitting its lowest since January 12 earlier in the session.

Comments after the talks by Putin, who ruled out negotiations for a Black Sea ceasefire after Ukraine destroyed part of a bridge linking Russia to Crimea, dampened hopes of progress towards de-escalation in the conflict that has stifled grain trade and crimped supplies from the region.

CBOT January soybean futures fell 9-1/4 cents to $12.07-1/2 a bushel after hitting overhead technical resistance at its 20-day moving average and breaching chart support at its 200-day average.

Soybeans were pressured by the weakening Brazilian real , which tends to trigger greater farmer sales there.

Favourable weather in Brazil has also anchored the soybean market after what is estimated to be a record US harvest.

The market has also been watching for developments in US-Chinese trade relations, in which agricultural purchases are a major issue, after discussions between Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping during an Asia-Pacific summit.

data.title: License information for AI chips sent to China released by US House committee
data.description:
The US Commerce Department approved shipments of nearly 900,000 advanced AI chips for Chinese companies through May 2026, the House Foreign Affairs Committee said on Thursday.

The committee said in a statement that its Republican chairman, Brian Mast, had "exercised his authorities under the Export Control Reform Act to publicly reveal export control license application information regarding NVIDIA and AMD's AI chip licenses for the People's Republic of China."

The committee said that its findings included "requested sales of 3.4 million AI chips to China, and the approval of more than 879,000 by BIS-including approvals for AI chip exports to Department of War-designated Chinese Military Companies like Alibaba and Tencent. It also includes requests by NVIDIA to depend on possible chip-smuggling fronts to facilitate their sales of advanced AI chips to Chinese companies."

data.title: Japanese investors sought $9.4 billion of shares in Anthropic IPO, sources say
data.description:
By Anton Bridge and Miho Uranaka

Japanese investors sought to buy more than 1.5 trillion yen ($9.40 billion) worth of Anthropic shares at its public listing this week, two people familiar with the offer said.

Japanese investors ultimately secured $2.98 billion worth of the shares, a filing showed on Thursday.

Anthropic raised $81 billion in total worldwide in what became the world's largest initial public offering on record, eclipsing SpaceX , which raised $75 billion at its listing in June.

Market sentiment has turned against AI-related firms in recent months, which sparked speculation that the Claude developer's listing would struggle to win over investors.

Anthropic ultimately priced its offering at $83 per share, above its initial range of $70 to $78.

Some Japanese investors saw Anthropic as the frontrunner among AI firms and so justified large orders, said the people, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to discuss the ​IPO publicly.

Other investors sought smaller allocations or sat out the offering altogether, seeing greater prospective returns in semiconductor stocks that have fallen sharply, such as Nvidia and Kioxia , or in waiting for OpenAI’s listing due next year, one of the people said.

More than 1,000 individuals sought allotments over 100 million yen, according to a demand survey by Mizuho Securities, part of Mizuho Financial Group , which was among the underwriters of the IPO and arranged the sale of the majority of shares sold in Japan. These applications totalled around 200 billion yen, the survey showed.

($1 = 159.5700 yen)
